decomposition.reasoning: Classic Latin compound. trans- ("across") is a highly productive English prefix (transform, transcend, transfer). port- ("carry") from Latin portāre is equally productive (export, import, portable, porter). Both morphemes are immediately recognizable and useful to a learner.

Classic Latin compound: ex- ("out/from") + port- ("carry", from portāre). Both morphemes are highly productive in modern English. ex- appears in export, exclude, exhale, emit; port- appears in transport, import, portable, deportation. A textbook decomposition with no false-root risk.

From Latin importare (im- "in/into" + portare "to carry"), meaning to carry something in — hence "to matter" or "to be of consequence". The root port- is highly productive in English (transport, export, portable, report). The prefix im- is a variant of in- before labial consonants. The suffix -ant is a standard Latin participial suffix forming adjectives/nouns. All three morphemes are live and recognizable to learners.

Classic Latin formation: port- (carry, from portāre) + -able (capable of being). Both morphemes are highly productive in modern English. Port- appears in transport, import, export, porter, portfolio; -able appears in hundreds of English adjectives (readable, flexible, visible). Straightforward and unambiguous.

The word "prognosis" is a direct borrowing from Greek prognōsis, composed of the prefix pro- (before/forward) + the root gnos- (know, from gnōsis) + the Greek noun-forming suffix -is. All three morphemes are productive and recognizable: pro- appears in prognosis, prognose, prolog, prophesy; gnos- appears in diagnosis, agnostic, cognition (via Latin), gnosis; -is is a common Greek noun suffix. This is a high-confidence decomposition.

From Greek diagnōsis: dia- (through/apart) + gnōsis (knowing). Both morphemes are productive and recognizable in modern English. The gno-/gnos- root appears in many English words (agnostic, prognosis, cognition via Latin cognoscere). The -e at the end is a standard English verb-forming ending added when the noun "diagnosis" was back-formed into the verb "diagnose". Confidence is high.

decomposition.meaning: relating to, having the quality of

decomposition.reasoning: The word "agnostic" is a well-known Greek compound: a- (not/without) + gnos- (know) + -tic (adjectival suffix). All three morphemes are productive and recognizable in modern English. The root gnos- appears in many English words (diagnosis, prognosis, cognitive via Latin cognoscere, gnosis, agnosia), and the prefix a- meaning "not/without" is extremely productive (amoral, atypical, asexual). The suffix -tic is a standard Greek-derived adjectival suffix (diagnostic, hypnotic, chaotic). The word was coined by T.H. Huxley in 1869 as a deliberate Greek formation, so the morphemes were never "fused" into an opaque unit — the composition is transparent and intentional.

Classic Greek compound: tele- (far) + phon- (sound/voice). Both morphemes are highly productive in modern English — tele- appears in television, telescope, telepathy; phon- appears in microphone, phonetics, symphony. The trailing -e is a nominal ending. Straightforward and unambiguous.

Two productive Greek roots: photo- (light) appears in photosynthesis, photon, photography; graph- (write/record) appears in paragraph, biography, telegram. The word literally means "written/recorded by light", which is a perfect description of how early photography worked. Both roots are highly recognizable and productive in modern English.

Classic Greek compound. bio- ("life") is a highly productive root seen in biography, biosphere, antibiotic, etc. log- ("study/reason/word") is equally productive in geology, psychology, ecology, etc. The -y suffix nominalises the compound. No connective vowel is needed here because bio- already ends in -o. Decomposition is unambiguous and etymologically transparent.

Two highly productive Greek roots: bio- (life) as in biology, biosphere, antibiotic, and graph- (write/record) as in photograph, paragraph, autograph. The noun-forming suffix -y is standard. Note: bio- already ends in -o, so no separate connective vowel is needed. Straightforward and unambiguous decomposition.

decomposition.meaning: relating to / of the nature of

decomposition.reasoning: Clear Greek compound: anti- ("against") + bio- ("life") + -tic (adjectival suffix meaning "relating to"). All three morphemes are productive and recognizable in modern English. anti- appears in antisocial, antibody, antidote; bio- appears in biology, biography, biosphere; -tic appears in acoustic, narcotic, symbiotic. The word literally means "against life" (i.e., destructive to living microorganisms).

Two highly productive Greek roots: geo- (earth) as in geology, geopolitics, geothermal; and graph- (write/record/describe) as in photograph, paragraph, autograph. The -y suffix nominalises the compound. No connective vowel is needed here because "geo" already ends in -o, which merges naturally with "graph". Straightforward, unambiguous decomposition.

Classic Greek compound: geo- (earth) + connective vowel -o- + log- (study/reason) + -y (noun-forming suffix). Both roots are highly productive in modern English: geo- appears in geography, geometry, geopolitics; log-/logy appears in biology, psychology, technology. The connective vowel -o- is emitted as a separate morpheme to keep both roots cleanly visible.

Classic Greek compound: therm- (heat) + connective vowel -o- + metr- (measure). Both roots are highly productive in modern English. therm- appears in thermal, thermostat, hypothermia; metr-/meter appears in barometer, speedometer, geometry. The connective -o- is the standard Greek linking vowel and should be emitted separately so both roots remain clean and recognizable to the learner.

A Greek-Latin hybrid compound: tele- (Greek, "far") + vis (Latin root of vidēre, "to see") + -ion (Latin nominalising suffix). All three morphemes are highly productive in English: tele- appears in telephone, telescope, telepathy; vis- appears in vision, visible, visual, evidence; -ion appears in countless English nouns. The decomposition clearly maps to the word's meaning: "the act of seeing at a distance."

Classic Greek compound: micro- (small) + connective vowel -o- + scop- (look/examine) + noun-forming -e. Both roots are highly productive in modern English: micro- appears in microphone, microbe, microchip; scop- appears in telescope, periscope, stethoscope. The decomposition is etymologically clean and pedagogically valuable.

Classic Greek compound: auto- (self) + graph- (write). Both morphemes are highly productive in modern English. auto- appears in automobile, autonomous, autocrat, autobiography; graph- appears in photograph, paragraph, biography, telegram. The meaning "self-write" maps directly and transparently onto the modern word's meaning (a signature written by oneself). No connective vowel needed here as auto- already ends in -o.

Classic Greek compound: cardi- (heart, from kardia) + connective vowel -o- + log- (study/reason, from logos) + noun-forming suffix -y. All morphemes are productive in modern English: cardi- appears in cardiac, cardiovascular, tachycardia; -o- is the standard Greek connective vowel; log-/logy appears in biology, psychology, geology, and dozens more. Straightforward, high-confidence decomposition.

A straightforward Greek compound: derm-/dermat- (skin) + connective vowel -o- + log- (study/reason) + -y (nominalizing suffix). All four morphemes are productive in modern English: derm- appears in epidermis, hypodermic; -logy appears in biology, psychology, geology, and dozens more. Classic "study of skin" formation.

Two productive Greek roots: paed-/ped- (child) as seen in pedagogy, and iatr- (physician/heal) as seen in psychiatry, geriatrics. They are joined by the connective vowel -i-, and the adjectival suffix -ic is added. All morphemes are well-known and productive in modern English medical vocabulary.

Two highly productive Greek roots (dem- = people, crat- = rule/power) joined by the standard Greek connective vowel -o-, with the nominalising suffix -y. Both roots are widely productive in English: dem- appears in epidemic, endemic, demography; crat- appears in aristocrat, autocrat, bureaucrat, technocrat. A textbook example of a clean, learnable Greek compound.

Two highly productive Greek roots joined by the standard connective vowel -o-. phil- (love) appears in philanthropy, bibliophile, philharmonic; soph- (wisdom) appears in sophisticated, sophomore. The -y suffix nominalises the compound. Unambiguous and well-attested.

A classic Greek compound: phil- (love) + connective vowel -o- + anthrop- (human being) + noun-forming suffix -y. All morphemes are productive and well-attested in modern English. phil- appears in philosophy, bibliophile, philharmonic; anthrop- appears in anthropology, misanthropy, anthropomorphic.

Clear Greek compound: chron- (time, from Greek chronos) + -ic (adjectival suffix meaning "relating to"). Both morphemes are productive in modern English. chron- appears in chronology, synchronize, anachronism; -ic appears in dozens of English adjectives (historic, democratic, economic).

Two highly productive Greek roots joined by the standard Greek connective vowel -o-. chron- (time) appears in synchronize, anachronism, chronic, chronicle; log- (study/word/reason) appears in biology, geology, psychology, logic. The -y suffix nominalises the compound. Straightforward and unambiguous.

All three morphemes are productive in modern English: syn- appears in synthesis, symphony, synonym; chron- appears in chronology, anachronism, chronic; -ize appears in modernize, capitalize, nationalize. The decomposition is etymologically sound and immediately useful to a learner.

Hydrogen is a well-established compound from Greek hydro- (water) + gen- (produce/origin), literally "water-producer" — named because burning hydrogen produces water. Both roots are highly productive in modern English: hydro- appears in hydrology, dehydrate, hydroelectric; gen- appears in generate, genesis, oxygen, nitrogen. The connective vowel -o- is emitted as a separate morpheme to keep both roots cleanly visible.

From French oxygène, coined by Lavoisier from Greek oxys (sharp, acid) + genēs (producing). The name reflects the (mistaken) belief that oxygen is essential to all acids. Both roots are productive in modern English: oxy- appears in oxide, oxymoron, oxyacid; gen- appears in generate, genesis, hydrogen, pathogen. No connective vowel needed here as the roots are directly joined.

The word "genesis" comes directly from Greek "genesis" (origin, creation), built from the root gen- (birth, origin) and the Greek noun-forming suffix -esis (process/act of). The root gen- is highly productive in English: genetics, generate, pathogen, hydrogen, genre, genealogy. The suffix -esis also appears in other English words like synthesis, thesis, and parenthesis. This is a clean, high-confidence decomposition.

From Latin dictionarium, built on dict- (say/tell, from dicere) + -ion (nominalising suffix) + -ary (relating to / place for). The root dict- is highly productive in English: dictate, predict, diction, verdict, contradict. The suffixes -ion and -ary are both common and independently recognisable. The combination dict + -ion gives "diction" (manner of speaking), and -ary then turns it into "a place/collection relating to diction/words".

Classic Latin compound: pre- (before) + dict- (say/tell, from Latin dicere). Both morphemes are highly productive in modern English. pre- appears in prefix, prepare, prevent, preview; dict- appears in dictate, verdict, contradict, diction, edict. A learner who sees this decomposition gains real insight into both morphemes.

Classic Latin compound: contra- (against) + dict- (say, from dicere). Both morphemes are highly productive in modern English. contra- appears in contrary, contraband, contraceptive; dict- appears in dictate, predict, verdict, diction, dictionary. The meaning "speak against" maps transparently onto the modern sense of the word.

From Anglo-French and Medieval Latin "veredictum" — literally "truly said" or "true saying." Both roots are productive in modern English: ver- appears in verify, veracity, verity; dict- appears in dictate, predict, diction, contradict. Clean two-root Latin compound with no affixes needed.

A clean Latin compound: manus (hand) + scriptus (written). Both roots are highly productive in modern English: manu- appears in manual, manufacture, manipulate, manicure; script- appears in scripture, prescribe, describe, transcript. The compound literally means "written by hand", which is transparent and historically accurate. High confidence.

The word "description" comes from Latin descriptio, built from de- (down/thoroughly) + scribere (to write) + -tio (noun-forming suffix). The root scrib-/script- is highly productive in English (describe, prescribe, manuscript, subscribe, inscription). The suffix -tion is one of the most common Latin nominalizing suffixes in English. Note: the surface form shows "scrip" rather than "scrib" due to the Latin consonant shift before -t (scrib- → script- before -tion), which is a regular pattern seen in prescription, inscription, subscription. Confidence is high.

Clear Latin compound: in- (into/upon) + script (written, past participle stem of scribere "to write") + -ion (nominalizing suffix). All three morphemes are highly productive in modern English: in- appears in include, inscribe, insert; script/scrib- appears in describe, prescription, manuscript, scripture; -ion appears in action, construction, education. The meaning "act of writing upon (something)" is fully transparent from its parts.

Two highly productive Greek roots joined by the standard connective vowel -o-. psych- (mind/soul) appears in psychiatry, psychosis, psyche; log- (study/reason) appears in biology, geology, logic, catalogue. The -y suffix nominalises the compound. Straightforward and well-known decomposition.

The word "memorial" clearly breaks down into the Latin root mem- (memory/mind) + the noun-forming suffix -or (giving "memoria" / "memory") + the adjectival suffix -ial (relating to). All three morphemes are productive in modern English: mem- appears in memory, remember, commemorate; -or appears in honor, error, terror; -ial appears in industrial,atorial, editorial. The decomposition is etymologically sound and learner-friendly.

From Latin memoria, built on the adjective memor ("mindful, remembering"), itself from the root mem- (mind, memory). The -y suffix nominalizes it. The root mem- is productive in English: remember, memorial, memorize, commemorate, memorandum. High confidence decomposition.

False-root trap. "Uncle" looks like it could be parsed as "un-" + "-cle", but this is entirely misleading. The word comes from Latin "avunculus" (mother's brother), itself a diminutive of "avus" (grandfather). The word entered English via Old French "oncle". There are no separable productive morphemes here — the surface form is simply a phonological reduction of the borrowed Latin/French stem. Teaching "un- + cle" would be a falsehood.

False-root trap. "Island" looks like it could be decomposed as "is-" + "land", but the "s" was never a meaningful morpheme. The word derives from Old English "iegland" (ieg = island/watery land + land), and the "s" was inserted in the 16th century through folk-etymological influence from the unrelated Latin-derived word "isle" (from Latin "insula"). The surface form is historically misleading, and no productive decomposition exists. Refusing to avoid teaching a false analogy.

False-root trap. "Butter" looks like it could be "butt" + "-er" (agent suffix, "one who butts"), but it is actually borrowed from Greek "boutyron" via Latin "butyrum". The "-er" ending is simply part of the borrowed stem, not a productive English agent suffix. No reliable decomposition is possible.

Two productive Greek roots joined by the standard Greek connective vowel -o-. crypt- (hidden) appears in words like crypt, cryptic, encrypt, apocryphal. graph- (write) appears in photography, paragraph, autograph, telegram. The -y suffix nominalises the compound. Straightforward Greek formation.

A clean Greek compound of two productive roots (xen- "stranger" and phob- "fear") joined by the standard Greek connective vowel -o-, plus the Greek nominal suffix -ia forming a condition/state noun. Both roots are highly productive in English: xen- appears in xenophile, xenon; phob- appears in phobia, claustrophobia, agoraphobia, and many more. The connective -o- is emitted as its own morpheme to keep both flanking roots cleanly visible.

Classic Latin compound. omni- ("all") is a productive English prefix (omnipotent, omniscient, omnipresent). The root vor- ("devour/eat") from Latin vorāre is also productive and recognizable in English words like carnivore, herbivore, voracious, and devour. The final -e is a standard noun-forming ending from the Latin agent/class noun. Clean, learnable decomposition with no false-root traps.

Classic Latin compound. "Herba" (grass/plant) + connective -i- + "vorare" (to devour) + noun-forming -e. Both roots are productive in English: herb- appears in herbal, herbicide, herbaceous; vor- appears in carnivore, omnivore, voracious, devour. The connective -i- is a standard Latin linking vowel used in compounds of this type.

Classic Latin compound. carn- (flesh) is productive in English: carnival, incarnate, carnal, carnage. vor- (devour) is productive in English: voracious, herbivore, omnivore, devour. The connecting -i- is a standard Latin linking vowel between compound elements. The final -e is a noun-forming ending inherited from Latin carnivorus (via French). High confidence: the learner can immediately connect carn- and vor- to many other English words.

decomposition.meaning: having the quality of, inclined to

decomposition.reasoning: From Latin benevolens (well-wishing): bene- (well/good) + vol- (wish/will, from velle) + -ent (adjectival suffix). All three morphemes are productive and recognizable in English. bene- appears in benefit, benefactor, beneficent; vol- appears in volunteer, volition, malevolent; -ent appears in dependent, fluent, evident.

decomposition.meaning: having the quality of, characterized by

decomposition.reasoning: From Latin malevolens: male- (bad/evil, from malus) + vol- (wish/will, from velle) + -ent (adjectival suffix). All three morphemes are productive and recognizable in modern English. male-/mal- appears in malfunction, malice, malformed; vol- appears in volunteer, volition, benevolent; -ent appears in dependent, confident, etc. The opposite benevolent (bene- + vol- + -ent) provides a perfect contrast that reinforces all three parts.

The word "renovate" comes directly from Latin renovare (re- = again + novare = to make new, from novus = new). All three morphemes are productive in modern English: re- appears in rebuild, reconsider, reform; nov- appears in novel, innovate, novice, novelty; -ate appears in create, activate, generate. Clean, high-confidence decomposition.
